title: The Boeing Company FY2022 Form 10-K — Item 1. Business: reportable segments and segment descriptions
key_points: Boeing states it is organized based on the products and services it offers and operates in FOUR reportable segments: Commercial Airplanes (BCA), Defense, Space & Security (BDS), Global Services (BGS), and Boeing Capital (BCC).

BCA 'develops, produces and markets commercial jet aircraft principally to the commercial airline industry worldwide', offering jetliners for passenger and cargo requirements of airlines; in-production family is the 737 narrow-body plus 767, 777 and 787 wide-bodies; 747 wide-body production ended in 2022; 777X and 737-7/737-10 remain in development.

BDS engages in research, development, production and modification of manned and unmanned military aircraft and weapons systems (fighter/trainer aircraft, rotorcraft and tilt-rotor), commercial derivative aircraft including anti-submarine and tanker aircraft, strategic missile and defense systems, C4ISR, cyber and intelligence systems, and satellite systems including government and commercial satellites and space exploration.
BGS 'provides services to our commercial and defense customers worldwide' (segment description text is truncated in the retrieved chunk after 'BGS sustains aerosp...').

BCC 'seeks to ensure that Boeing customers have the financing they need to buy and take delivery of their Boeing product, while managing overall financing exposure'; its portfolio consists of equipment under operating leases, sales-type/finance leases, notes and other receivables, assets held for sale or re-lease and investments.
raw_excerpt: We are organized based on the products and services we offer. We operate in four reportable segments: • Commercial Airplanes (BCA); • Defense, Space & Security (BDS); • Global Services (BGS); • Boeing Capital (BCC). Commercial Airplanes Segment This segment develops, produces and markets commercial jet aircraft principally to the commercial airline industry worldwide. ... BCC seeks to ensure that Boeing customers have the financing they need to buy and take delivery of their Boeing product, while managing overall financing exposure.

key_points: Note 1 independently confirms the four-segment structure: 'we operate in four reportable segments: Commercial Airplanes (BCA), Defense, Space & Security (BDS), Global Services (BGS) and Boeing Capital (BCC).'
The same note discloses 2022 segment revenues: BCA $25,867M, BDS $23,162M, BGS $17,611M, BCC $199M, Unallocated items/eliminations $(231)M, total $66,608M.

Note 1 describes BCA revenue as derived mostly from commercial aircraft contracts, and long-term service contract sales as primarily support and maintenance agreements associated with commercial and defense products plus space travel on Commercial Crew.

title: Boeing FY2022 10-K — MD&A Overview: company positioning and segment roles
key_points: Boeing describes itself as one of the two major manufacturers of 100+ seat airplanes for the worldwide commercial airline industry and one of the largest defense contractors in the U.S.
BGS 'provides support for commercial and defense through innovative, comprehensive and cost-competitive product and service solutions.'
BCC 'facilitates, arranges, structures and provides selective financing solutions for our Boeing customers.'

The 10-K refers to 'our airline customers' in North and South America, the Middle East and Europe, and separately notes that the war in Ukraine continues to impact 'our airline and lessor customers' — distinguishing airlines from lessors as customer groups.
raw_excerpt: We are one of the two major manufacturers of 100+ seat airplanes for the worldwide commercial airline industry and one of the largest defense contractors in the U.S. ... BGS provides support for commercial and defense through innovative, comprehensive and cost-competitive product and service solutions. BCC facilitates, arranges, structures and provides selective financing solutions for our Boeing customers. ... The war in Ukraine continues to impact our airline and lessor customers.

title: Boeing FY2022 10-K — BCA segment MD&A: customer geography and backlog concentration
key_points: Approximately 70% of Commercial Airplanes' total backlog, in dollar terms, is with non-U.S. airlines.

BCA faces international competitors (Airbus, including the A220 in the 100-150 seat market, and COMAC, which delivered its first C919 in 2022) that have access to most of the same customers and suppliers.
raw_excerpt: Approximately 70% of Commercial Airplanes' total backlog, in dollar terms, is with non-U.S. airlines. We face aggressive international competitors who are intent on increasing their market share. They offer competitive products and have access to most of the same customers and suppliers.

key_points: At the end of 2022, 28% of BDS backlog was attributable to non-U.S. customers.

BDS demand is framed around U.S. DoD, NASA and other government agencies: the FY23 Consolidated Appropriations Act provided $817 billion for the U.S. DoD and $25.4 billion for NASA, including funding for Boeing programs such as F/A-18, F-15EX, CH-47, AH-64, V-22, KC-46A, MQ-25 and the Space Launch System.

title: Boeing FY2022 10-K — BGS segment MD&A: U.S. government as BGS's major customer
key_points: The 10-K explicitly labels the U.S. government as BGS's 'major customer'.
The U.S. government services market is described as the single largest individual market, comprising over 50 percent of the government services markets served by BGS.
BGS 2022 revenue was $17,611M, 26% of total company revenues, with earnings from operations of $2,727M (15.5% operating margin).
BGS revenue drivers are described in terms of 'commercial services volume' versus 'government services volume', reflecting the two customer tracks.

The U.S. government services market is the single largest individual market, comprising over 50 percent of the government services markets served.

title: Boeing FY2022 10-K — Note 9 Customer Financing and BCC portfolio concentration risk
key_points: Customer financing primarily relates to the BCC segment; financing arrangements typically range from 1 to 12 years and may include options to extend or terminate the lease, and certain leases allow the lessee to purchase the underlying aircraft at a specified price.

Customer financing at December 31, 2022 totaled $1,604M, comprising financing receivables of $1,189M (sales-type/finance leases $804M, notes $385M) less allowance of $55M, plus operating lease equipment of $470M.

At December 31, 2022, $405M of financing receivables were determined to be uncollectible and placed on non-accrual status; the increase in the allowance was primarily due to impacts of the war in Ukraine.

Certain leases include provisions to allow the lessee to purchase the underlying aircraft at a specified price. ... Total $1,604 $1,812

title: Boeing FY2022 10-K — Risk Factors: concentration of customer financing portfolio among certain customers
key_points: A significant portion of Boeing's customer financing portfolio is concentrated among certain customers and in distinct geographic regions, and across Boeing aircraft product types (most notably 717 and 747-8), including customers believed to have less than investment-grade credit.
The risk factor describes defaults or non-renewal of leases by such customers as a material risk, indicating that lessees (leasing customers) are a distinct customer relationship type for Boeing.
raw_excerpt: A significant portion of our customer financing portfolio is concentrated among certain customers and in distinct geographic regions. Our portfolio is also concentrated by varying degrees across Boeing aircraft product types, most notably 717 and 747-8 aircraft, and among customers that we believe have less than investment-grade credit.

title: Boeing FY2022 10-K — Risk Factors: dependence on major commercial airline customers
key_points: The 10-K refers to 'our major commercial airline customers' as a distinct customer group whose fleet decisions, consolidations or financial challenges could significantly reduce revenues.
raw_excerpt: In addition, fleet decisions, airline consolidations or financial challenges involving any of our major commercial airline customers could significantly reduce our revenues and limit our opportunity to generate profits from those customers.

title: Boeing FY2022 10-K — Note 22 / Unallocated items: BCC aircraft sales and intersegment treatment
key_points: Unallocated items, eliminations and other include intercompany guarantees provided to BCC and eliminations of certain sales between segments, including aircraft sold to the BCC segment that are leased by BCC to customers and considered transferred to the BCC segment.
This confirms BCC acts as a leasing intermediary between Boeing and end customers (lessees).
raw_excerpt: Unallocated items, eliminations and other include common internal services that support Boeing's global business operations, intercompany guarantees provided to BCC and eliminations of certain sales between segments. Such sales include aircraft sold to our BCC segment that are leased by BCC to customers and considered transferred to the BCC segment.

title: Boeing FY2022 Form 10-K — Backlog conversion expectations (p116)
key_points: Of the $404,381M total backlog at December 31, 2022, approximately 17% is expected to convert to revenue through 2023 and approximately 71% through 2026, with the remainder thereafter.

Boeing cites significant uncertainty on backlog conversion timing due to 787 deliveries from inventory, 737 MAX delivery resumption in China, 777X/737-7/737-10 entry into service, and lingering COVID-19 effects.

title: Boeing FY2022 10-K — Item 1 Business: segment structure and customer types (p.3)
key_points: Boeing operates in four reportable segments: Commercial Airplanes (BCA), Defense, Space & Security (BDS), Global Services (BGS), and Boeing Capital (BCC).
BCA offers a family of commercial jetliners (737 narrow-body; 767, 777, 787 wide-body) designed to meet requirements of airlines; 747 production ended in 2022.
BDS engages in research, development, production and modification of manned and unmanned military aircraft and weapons systems for strike, surveillance and mobility.
The 10-K describes customer categories generically (airlines, government customers) and does not enumerate named customers in Item 1.

title: BOEING_2022_10K — FY23 U.S. appropriations funding Boeing programs
key_points: The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023 (enacted December 2022) provided $817B for the U.S. DoD and $25.4B for NASA.
FY23 appropriations included funding for Boeing's F/A-18 Super Hornet, F-15EX, CH-47 Chinook, AH-64 Apache, V-22 Osprey, KC-46A Tanker, MQ-25 and Space Launch System programs.
FY23 appropriations supported F/A-18 production further into calendar year 2025 and did not include funding for additional P-8 aircraft.

title: BOEING_2022_10K — Named government customers: USAF (KC-46A) and NASA (Commercial Crew)
key_points: In 2011 Boeing was awarded a USAF contract to design, develop, manufacture and deliver four next-generation aerial refueling tankers plus priced options for 13 annual production lots totaling 179 aircraft.

Since 2016 the USAF has authorized eight low-rate initial production (LRIP) lots for a total of 109 aircraft; the EMD contract and authorized LRIP lots total approximately $21B as of December 31, 2022.
NASA has contracted Boeing to design and build the CST-100 Starliner spacecraft to transport crews to the International Space Station.

The EMD contract and authorized LRIP lots total approximately $21 billion as of December 31, 2022. … NASA has contracted us to design and build the CST-100 Starliner spacecraft to transport crews to the International Space Station.

title: BOEING_2022_10K — Third-party industry demand data cited from IATA
key_points: Per IATA (as cited in the 10-K), airline industry net losses were $138B in 2020 and $42B in 2021.
IATA forecast $6.9B of global industry losses for 2022, with approximately $9.9B of profits in North America offset by losses in other regions.
IATA forecast $4.6B of global industry profits for 2023.
This is Boeing's citation of IATA data, not a directly read IATA report, and it describes industry profitability rather than Boeing's customer mix.
raw_excerpt: According to the International Air Transport Association (IATA), net losses for the airline industry were $138 billion in 2020 and $42 billion in 2021. IATA also forecasts $6.9 billion of losses for the industry globally in 2022, with approximately $9.9 billion of profits in North America driven by the robust domestic market being more than offset by losses in other regions. For 2023, IATA is forecasting $4.6 billion in profits for the industry globally.
